summary: This memo is a policy statement on introducing the Domain Style Naming System. It partly updates RFC 881 and sets the schedule for hosts to switch to domain-style names, starting on 14 March 1984, after which old-style names would be dropped.

eli5.summary: The network announced a date when everyone must start using the new kind of names, and later stop using the old ones.

subtitle: The 1984 timetable for moving every host from flat names to hierarchical domain-style names.

tldr.problem: Hosts had flat names and found addresses by copying a central table kept at the NIC. That would not scale as the Internet grew.
tldr.mechanism: The memo sets a dated plan: first add the .ARPA suffix to old names, then add domains and name servers, then allow multi-part and organization names, and finally retire the central table.
tldr.outcome: It is an official policy statement of the ICCB and DARPA that partly updates RFC 881, and it was itself updated by RFC 921.

today: This memo is a dated policy for 1984 that partly updates RFC 881, and the metadata lists it as updated by RFC 921. Its own schedule has long since passed, and the text says nothing about later events.

sections.title: The Current Situation
sections.content:
RFC 897 is a policy statement of the ICCB and DARPA about implementing the Domain Style Naming System. It partly updates RFC 881 and leaves the explanation of how the system works to the references.

At the time, hosts in the ARPA research and DDN operational communities had names in a flat, global space, such as USC-ISIF. A name must start with a letter, end with a letter or digit, and use only letters, digits or hyphens inside, and case is not significant. Translating a name to an address was done by looking it up in a table of all hosts, maintained centrally at the Network Information Center (NIC), and each host was expected to fetch a current copy on time.

Mail to other systems hid foreign addressing in the local part, with a mail-relay host as the host part, for example EDMISTON.CIC@CSNET-RELAY.
sections.eli5: Everyone's name was on one big list kept in one place, and each computer had to copy the list to find its friends.

sections.title: The Future Situation: Hierarchical Names and Servers
sections.content:
Because the Internet is growing, names become structured: each element is a string with the old constraints, as in F.ISI.USC.ARPA. Translation will be done by interacting with a service, with a number of servers each holding a portion of the data, and maintenance of the data will be subdivided and distributed.

The memo describes three stages of use. First, domain names simply replace host names, with two components, such as USC-ISIF.ARPA or USC-ISIA.DDN. Second, names get more components, such as F.ISI.USC.ARPA. Third, names may stand for organizations rather than hosts, so finding a mail host may need one level of indirection: asking the server about USC-ISI.ARPA returns a real host such as F.USC-ISI.ARPA, and mail goes to its SMTP port.
sections.eli5: Instead of one long list, names get several parts, like street, city and country, and many helpers each know about their own part.

sections.title: The Transition Plan and Policy
sections.content:
Two changes happen at once: the way names are translated (from local copies of a central table to dynamic lookups against distributed servers) and the names themselves (from a flat space to a hierarchy). The plan has four steps: change old names to domain style (host-name becomes host-name.ARPA), go from one domain to a few such as ARPA and DDN, switch from central tables to name servers, then allow many domains.

The ARPA research community makes the whole transition. The DDN operational community changes names on the same schedule but is not required to adopt servers at the same time; the DDN PMO will set that schedule later, and the NIC will keep a central table of DDN hosts.

The policy statement: hosts begin using domain style names on 14-Mar-84, and old style names will be completely phased out before 2-May-84. Because every host changes name, old names are kept as nicknames for a while, and it must stay possible to find a host's primary name from its Internet address.
sections.eli5: Everyone starts by adding the same short ending to their old name, so nobody gets lost. Then, step by step, the new system with helpers takes over from the big list.

sections.title: The Time Table
sections.content:
The memo gives a dated list of milestones. RFC 881 published the plan in November 1983, together with the draft protocol and database design in RFC 882 and RFC 883, and a domain-style host table (DHOSTS.TXT) became available.

On 14 March 1984 hosts begin using domain names as official names. On 4 April 1984 several servers for the ARPA domain start, one at the NIC, and a master table of top-level domains is set up there. On 2 May 1984 old names stop and a few new domains such as DDN may appear. On 6 June 1984 more domains may be created and names may have more than two segments. On 18 July 1984 organizational domains are allowed. On 5 September 1984 the NIC's master host table no longer has to be complete for the ARPA community, and on 3 October 1984 the DDN PMO establishes its plan for name service.
sections.eli5: It is a calendar with a date for each step, from the first day of new names to the day the big list can retire.

events.label: 14 Mar: begin using domain style names
5 Sep: host table need not be complete
